title: US Slaps Sanctions on Iraq's Oil Boss, Says He Helped Iran Sneak Oil Past Rules
summary: Imagine if your neighbor was sneaking candy out of your house and selling it to break the rules. That's kind of what the United States says is happening with oil in the Middle East—but on a much bigger scale! On Thursday, the US Treasury sanctioned (which means punished by freezing money and blocking business) Iraq's Deputy Oil Minister, Ali Maarij al-Bahadly. They say he helped Iran sell its oil even though the US has rules against it. The US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, said Iran is acting "like a rogue gang" and stealing resources that belong to the Iraqi people. He said the money from the oil helps fund terrorism against the US and its friends. Iraq and Iran haven't said anything back yet. Al-Bahadly has been a big deal in Iraq's oil world for years. The US says he was right in the middle of a sneaky plan: Iranian oil tankers used fake Iraqi papers to hide where the oil really came from. Then they mixed it with Iraqi oil and sold it as if it was all from Iraq. Experts think Iran makes at least $1 billion a year from this trick. The US also sanctioned three other men tied to pro-Iran militias, saying they helped with oil smuggling and buying weapons. This all comes as the US and Iran are in a tense fight over the Strait of Hormuz, a super important waterway for oil shipments. The US has been putting more and more pressure on Iran, especially since the war with Israel started. It's a complicated story, but at its heart, it's about who controls the oil—and the money.
why_it_matters: Oil is turned into petrol for cars and buses, and many everyday things are made from it, so when oil gets involved in secret deals and fights, it can make fuel and other products more expensive for everyone.

background_read: The United States often uses sanctions—freezing money and blocking business—to pressure countries it disagrees with. The US Treasury is the government department that handles these punishments.
Iran and Iraq are neighbours in the Middle East. Both have large oil reserves, but the US and Iran have had a difficult relationship for many years, especially over Iran’s support for armed groups.
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman. Around one‑fifth of the world’s oil passes through it, so any tension there can affect fuel prices everywhere.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ali Maarij al‑Bahadly (Iraq’s Deputy Oil Minister), US Treasury, Iran
WHAT: The US sanctioned al‑Bahadly for helping Iran secretly sell oil by using fake Iraqi documents
WHERE: Iraq and Iran, with the oil travelling through the Strait of Hormuz
WHY: The US says Iran’s oil money funds terrorism and that smuggling steals from the Iraqi people

perspectives.description: Sees these sanctions as a necessary step to stop Iran from getting money that supports terrorism and to protect Iraq’s resources.
Likely views the sanctions as unfair foreign interference and may keep finding ways to sell oil to keep its economy going.
Some might be angry that officials helped a neighbour steal oil, while others might feel trapped between two powerful countries.
Worries that more tension in the Strait of Hormuz could block oil shipments and cause a worldwide jump in energy costs.
